genZNote: Rinse your contacts with tap water instead of solution and this is exactly the amoeba waiting in the pipes.

morphology.shape: Amoeboid trophozoite with characteristic spiny (acanthopodia) projections; double-walled cyst

lifeCycleStages: Cyst (environmentally resistant, no flagellate stage exists in this genus)

habitat.naturalHabitat: Ubiquitous in soil, freshwater, and even air; also found in tap water, swimming pools, and contact lens solutions/cases when contaminated
habitat.hostAssociation: Free-living; humans are accidental hosts, typically via contact lens use or minor trauma/immunosuppression
habitat.environmentalOccurrence: Extremely widespread environmental organism, more ubiquitous than Naegleria
habitat.reservoir: Soil, water, air, and contaminated contact lens equipment

microscopy.stain: Confocal microscopy or calcofluor white stain of corneal scrapings for keratitis; trichrome stain of tissue for encephalitis
microscopy.appearance: Trophozoites with spiny surface projections (acanthopodia); double-walled, star-shaped (polygonal) cysts
microscopy.arrangement: Trophozoites and cysts in corneal or CNS tissue

culture.media: Non-nutrient agar with an E. coli overlay
culture.growthCharacteristics: Grows on the bacterial lawn, forming trails of feeding trophozoites and resistant cysts
culture.colonyMorphology: Not applicable in the traditional sense

biochemicalTests.test: PCR of corneal scraping or CSF/tissue

identificationClues: History of contact lens wear, particularly with poor hygiene (tap water rinsing, swimming while wearing lenses, non-sterile lens solution)
Severe, often disproportionate eye pain with a corneal ring infiltrate on slit-lamp exam (Acanthamoeba keratitis)
No flagellate stage exists for this genus, unlike Naegleria, which has a transient flagellate form
Causes a much slower, more indolent CNS disease (granulomatous amoebic encephalitis) than the rapidly fatal course of Naegleria's PAM, typically in immunocompromised hosts

diseases: Acanthamoeba keratitis — painful corneal infection strongly associated with contact lens wear, which can cause severe vision loss if untreated
Granulomatous amoebic encephalitis (GAE) — a subacute-to-chronic CNS infection, mainly in immunocompromised patients
Cutaneous acanthamoebiasis, particularly in advanced HIV/AIDS
virulenceFactors: Adhesion to corneal epithelium via a mannose-binding protein, especially relevant to contact lens-associated keratitis
Ability to encyst under adverse conditions, making the organism resistant to many disinfectants and some antimicrobial treatments
clinicalImportance.transmission: Contact lens exposure to contaminated water/solution (keratitis); inhalation or skin/eye entry with subsequent hematogenous CNS spread (GAE), typically in immunocompromised hosts
clinicalImportance.epidemiology: The leading cause of contact-lens-associated keratitis; GAE is rare but classically affects immunocompromised patients (HIV/AIDS, transplant recipients) with a much more insidious onset than Naegleria's PAM
clinicalImportance.labSignificance: Contact lens wearers presenting with a painful, poorly responsive 'corneal ulcer' that isn't improving on standard antibacterial/antiviral therapy should raise suspicion for Acanthamoeba keratitis, prompting corneal scraping for confocal microscopy/culture/PCR

examFacts.keyBiochemicalReaction: Not applicable — diagnosed by corneal scraping microscopy/culture/PCR
examFacts.importantDisease: Acanthamoeba keratitis (contact lens-associated); granulomatous amoebic encephalitis in immunocompromised hosts
examFacts.importantTest: Corneal scraping for confocal microscopy/culture on non-nutrient agar with E. coli overlay
examFacts.distinguishingFeature: A ubiquitous free-living amoeba lacking a flagellate stage, classically linked to contact-lens-associated keratitis and a slower, chronic form of amoebic encephalitis than Naegleria
